item.title: Staff Post- Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

That's a neat article. Overall this one is rather self-contained. However, SCP-505's ink does have a more sinister implication in the tale Ganymede. A simple in-line link could bridge the two articles. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

SCP-505-1 also has an increased rate of spread through non-viscous fluids such as water, as would be expected of normal ink. Any contamination of the water table with SCP-505-1 must be prevented at all costs, due to the potential for an NK-class end-of-the-world scenario. It is unknown whether SCP-505-1's aforementioned property of an inversely proportional rate of spread will manifest in fluids, as experimentation with such high quantities of SCP-505-1 is strictly forbidden. Thus, any environmental SCP-505-1 contamination in water sources must be met with immediate damming and drainage into storage tanks of all affected areas.

To this:

SCP-505-1 also has an increased rate of spread through non-viscous fluids such as water, as would be expected of normal ink. Any contamination of the water table with SCP-505-1 must be prevented at all costs, due to the potential for an NK-class end-of-the-world scenario. It is unknown whether SCP-505-1's aforementioned property of an inversely proportional rate of spread will manifest in fluids, as experimentation with such high quantities of SCP-505-1 is strictly forbidden. Thus, any environmental SCP-505-1 contamination in water sources must be met with immediate damming and drainage into storage tanks of all affected areas.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.content:encoded:
So, I know it's been a while since someone pointed out that the duck picture has a watermark… but the duck picture has a watermark. Considering the number of excellent pictures I've seen taken down because their sources couldn't be determined (FaminePulse's recent frustrations spring to mind) it's a bit surprising to see this one still here given that it's explicitly sourced from someone who watermarked and copyrighted it. The picture was taken in 1971, so a lot depends on whether the original photographer renewed the copyright - according to this the copyright would have lapsed in 1999 if she didn't renew it, but if she did renew it it's good until 2055 or so.

Has anybody attempted to communicate with her? Even if she did renew the copyright she might very well be cool with it (especially since the watermark hasn't been edited out)

Downvoted. I do not understand what people like about this…

Big words! Gold standard containment method!

Seriously, there are a lot of multisyllabic words that seem to be used just to try sounding "more clinical" (which actually pushed it into "too clinical" territory for me), and so many minor grammatical errors it was kind of bothersome to read through.

I also don't like the "thing what can't be contained" aspect. There are very few entries I think can pull that off well, and flamethrowers seem like they'd do a well enough job with this I don't see how it isn't contained.

item.content:encoded:
Eh. I've never really liked this one. I was pretty much able to guess its effect from just looking at the images. Don't get me wrong, it's still written well, and it's descriptive, but it feels lacking to me. I guess I was just hoping that there would be more too it, something outside the object, or a twist in my expectations.

Actually, I will give it this: I was expecting super deadly ink. Maybe it would become sentient or something, and it's refreshing to see it be deadly through more mundane reasons, but that's all I can say. It's like I was expecting a jump-scare, but didn't get one. I was pleasantly surprised that there wasn't one at first, but then I was disappointed when I figured out nothing took its place… If that makes sense.

Something that bothers me - if this ink is so dangerous, why use a measly concentration of 4 molars of sodium hydroxide to combat it? Why not bury it in solid NaOH pellets, or use something close to the saturation concentration (27 M)?

Apart from that, from a logical standpoint (which might be silly, I know - assuming an anomalous item behaves in an easily understood way) shouldn't porous materials catalyze the growth, since they have an immense surface to volume ratio?

There, done. I hope this hasn't been done before, 'black fluid that kills things' seems a bit dubiously cliche if I think about it, but I tried to emphasis that it's just ordinary ink, I thought that might help.
